description_full: Trekor Metals Limited, a mining company, acquires and develops mineral properties. It explores for copper, molybdenum, gold, niobium, and silver deposits. The company's principal assets consist of 100% owned the Gibraltar mine located in south-central British Columbia; and the Florence Copper project in Arizona. The company was formerly known as Taseko Mines Limited and changed its name Trekor Metals Limited in June 2026. Trekor Metals Limited was incorporated in 1966 and is headquartered in Vancouver, Canada.

financial_summary: Trekor Metals Limited is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $2.5B market cap on $476M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +17% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.
The company is burning through $158M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
Accruals are elevated at -10.1% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.2× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 0.5× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Net dilution runs at 7.2% annually, transferring value from owners to stock-based comp, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 3% operating margin trails the Basic Materials median (10%) by 7pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.23x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+14.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.04 across 219 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 102% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 15% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 29% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 71% and a beta of 1.29, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 2.96 vs 5y 1.58), so read it loosely.
About $39.8M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 64% in the 2020 crash, 62% in the 2022 bear market and 91% in 2008.
val: On multiples it looks expensive against Basic Materials peers: P/E 46.3 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 1674% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of -6.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 0.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The Street target $10.43 on average, 50% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.9%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.16).
Earnings quality is a concern: a weak Piotroski score of 3/9 and high accruals (-10.1% of assets).
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.2x net debt to EBITDA ($134.7M of cash against $503.5M of debt), and interest cover is thin at 0.5x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.57 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 16.9% over 3 years and 13.5% over 5 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 16%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 8.1% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.5%, and institutions hold 54%.
Net share issuance leaves shareholder yield negative (-7.2%), diluting holders.
The share count has grown 4.4% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
